module.title: 4 · Event-study / dynamic DiD
module.summary: Estimate a separate effect for each period relative to treatment to test pre-trends and trace the effect's dynamics.

stages.title: From one number to a whole path
stages.html:
The event-study design

The 2×2 estimator collapses everything into a single before/after contrast. With a panel of many periods we can do better: estimate a separate treated-vs-control gap for every period, relative to a chosen baseline period (usually the last period before treatment).

We interact the treated dummy with a full set of time dummies. Picking period r as the reference, the coefficient on treatedₜ is:

θₜ = (treated − control gap in period t) − (treated − control gap in period r)

Plotting θₜ against t gives the event-study plot, the single most important diagnostic in modern DiD.

Key idea. Pre-treatment coefficients (t < treatment) should be near zero — that is your visual test of parallel trends. Post-treatment coefficients trace how the effect turns on and evolves.

stages.title: Reading leads and lags
stages.html:
Leads, lags, and the reference period

  • Leads (periods before treatment, t < T*): these are a falsification test. If parallel trends holds, the treated and control groups tracked each other beforehand, so the leads should hug zero. Leads that drift away from zero signal a pre-trend and undercut the design.
  • Reference period (t = T*−1): normalized to exactly 0 by construction. Every other coefficient is measured relative to it, so it has no error bar.
  • Lags (periods at/after treatment): the dynamic treatment effects. They might jump immediately, ramp up gradually, or fade out.

In statsmodels we use a panel and the formula y ~ C(time, Treatment(reference=r))*treated + C(unit), then read off the coefficients named ...:treated. The C(unit) term adds unit fixed effects, absorbing every time-invariant difference between units. (The standalone treated term is then collinear with the unit dummies and contributes nothing extra — the per-period interactions carry the identification.)

Key idea. Flat pre-period coefficients are necessary, not sufficient — but a clean event-study plot with near-zero leads is the strongest practical evidence a DiD can offer.

stages.title: Build a panel and run an event study
stages.note: Multi-period panel: treatment turns on at time 4 with true effect 3. We estimate per-period effects and plot leads & lags with 95% intervals. Pre-period coefficients should sit near zero.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, nunit, treat_time, ref = 8, 60, 4, 3
rows = []
for u in range(nunit):
    g = 1 if u < nunit//2 else 0        # first half treated
    ai = rng.normal(0, 1)               # unit fixed effect
    for t in range(T):
        eff = 3.0 if (g == 1 and t >= treat_time) else 0.0
        y = 5 + ai + 0.5*t + eff + rng.normal(0, 1)
        rows.append((u, t, g, y))
df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['unit','time','treated','y'])

res = smf.ols(f'y ~ C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))*treated + C(unit)', df).fit()
ts, est, se = [], [], []
for t in range(T):
    ts.append(t)
    if t == ref:
        est.append(0.0); se.append(0.0); continue
    k = f'C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))[T.{t}]:treated'
    est.append(res.params[k]); se.append(res.bse[k])

for t,e in zip(ts,est): print(f'period {t}: effect = {e:+.3f}')
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.errorbar(ts, est, yerr=[1.96*s for s in se], fmt='o-', color='#da9100', ecolor='#c9c6ac', capsize=3)
plt.axhline(0, color='#6f6b57', lw=1)
plt.axvline(treat_time-0.5, color='#af983f', ls='--', label='treatment starts')
plt.xlabel('period'); plt.ylabel('treated - control gap'); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title('Event study: leads near 0, lags near +3')

stages.title: Pre-trend vs. true effect in the event-study plot
stages.note: Add a true post-treatment ATT and a per-period pre-trend that breaks parallelism. Watch the LEADS lift off zero when you introduce a pre-trend — exactly the warning sign analysts look for.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, nunit, treat_time, ref = 8, 60, 4, 3
rows = []
for u in range(nunit):
    g = 1 if u < nunit//2 else 0
    ai = rng.normal(0,1)
    for t in range(T):
        eff = {{att}} if (g==1 and t>=treat_time) else 0.0
        trend = {{pretrend}}*t*g          # divergence in every period -> shows up in leads too
        y = 5 + ai + 0.5*t + trend + eff + rng.normal(0,1)
        rows.append((u,t,g,y))
df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['unit','time','treated','y'])
res = smf.ols(f'y ~ C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))*treated + C(unit)', df).fit()
ts, est, se = [], [], []
for t in range(T):
    ts.append(t)
    if t == ref:
        est.append(0.0); se.append(0.0); continue
    k = f'C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))[T.{t}]:treated'
    est.append(res.params[k]); se.append(res.bse[k])
pre = [est[t] for t in range(treat_time)]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.errorbar(ts, est, yerr=[1.96*s for s in se], fmt='o-', color='#da9100', ecolor='#c9c6ac', capsize=3)
plt.axhline(0, color='#6f6b57', lw=1)
plt.axvline(treat_time-0.5, color='#af983f', ls='--', label='treatment starts')
plt.xlabel('period'); plt.ylabel('treated - control gap'); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f'max |lead| = {max(abs(p) for p in pre):.2f}  (should be ~0 if valid)')

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: In an event-study plot, what is the purpose of inspecting the PRE-treatment (lead) coefficients?
choices: They test the parallel-trends assumption — they should be near zero
They measure how fast the effect fades out
stages.hint: Before treatment there can be no effect, so any nonzero value means something else is going on.
stages.explain: Leads capture treated-vs-control differences before treatment, where the effect must be zero. Near-zero leads support parallel trends; nonzero leads reveal a pre-trend that invalidates the design.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Why is the reference period's coefficient exactly 0 with no confidence interval?
choices: The effect happens to be zero there
Every other period is measured relative to it, so it is normalized to 0 by construction
Its standard error is too large to plot
Treatment has no effect in that period
stages.hint: All θₜ are differences relative to that one omitted period.
stages.explain: The reference (omitted) period is the baseline against which all other coefficients are defined, so it is mechanically 0 and carries no sampling uncertainty.

stages.title: Reading a significant lead
stages.prompt: Your event-study plot shows a pre-treatment (lead) coefficient that is large and statistically significant, well away from zero. What does this tell you?
choices: It is reassuring — a significant pre-period coefficient confirms the design is working
It is a warning — a nonzero lead signals a pre-trend that undercuts parallel trends
It measures how quickly the treatment effect fades after treatment
It sets the reference period, so it should be large by construction
why: Backwards: leads should hug zero. A significant lead is evidence AGAINST parallel trends, not for the design.
Leads are before treatment, where the effect is zero by definition — they cannot measure post-treatment dynamics.
The reference period is the one normalized to 0 with no error bar; it is not the lead you are reading.
stages.hint: Where the effect must be zero, a coefficient far from zero is bad news, not good.
stages.explain: The 'significant pre-trend is reassuring' trap. Leads sit before treatment, where the true effect is zero, so they should hug zero; a large significant lead is evidence the groups were already diverging — a pre-trend that invalidates the design. The tempting belief flips the logic of a falsification test: you want to fail to reject here, not to find significance. Boundary: flat (near-zero) leads are necessary but not sufficient — failing to reject a pre-trend makes parallelism plausible, it never proves the untestable post-period counterfactual.

stages.title: What the event-study plot tells you
stages.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about an event-study (dynamic DiD) plot are TRUE?
choices: Pre-treatment (lead) coefficients should be near zero if parallel trends holds
The reference period's coefficient is exactly 0 by construction, with no confidence interval
Post-treatment (lag) coefficients trace how the effect turns on and evolves over time
Flat pre-period leads prove the parallel-trends assumption holds in the post period
A statistically significant lead coefficient is reassuring evidence for the design
stages.hint: Two of the five are classic traps: one over-claims what flat leads prove, one misreads what a significant lead means.
stages.explain: The 'flat leads = proven parallelism' over-claim. True: leads near zero are the visual test of parallel trends; the reference period is mechanically 0 with no error bar; lags trace the dynamic effect. False trap 1 — flat pre-period leads are necessary but not sufficient: parallel trends in the post period is untestable, since the treated counterfactual is never observed, so leads make it plausible, not proven. False trap 2 — a significant lead is the opposite of reassuring; it signals a pre-trend. Boundary: the event-study only ever offers indirect, pre-period evidence — it can falsify the design but never certify the post-period counterfactual.
